author: Bjorn Ashfist, smith of the Lower Town
pages:
#Introduction

My father was a smith, and his father, and his father's father. Not one of them ever wrote a word down. I am breaking with tradition because I am tired of answering the same questions from every young fool who walks into my forge.

#Start Small

Everyone wants to make a great sword on their first day. Nobody wants to make a hundred iron daggers. But the hundred daggers are how you learn what the metal wants. Every piece you finish teaches your hands something your head cannot.

Iron first. Then steel. Then, when your arms ache and your eyes water from the smoke and you have stopped burning yourself every other day, the rarer metals.

#Tempering

A weapon straight from the forge is only half finished. Take it to the grindstone, or a blade to the sharpening wheel and armour to the workbench, and you can improve it well beyond what the forge gave you. The more skilled your hands, the finer the result.

Tempered gear is worth more coin, too. Merchants can tell the difference, even when they pretend they cannot.

#On Rare Metals

The finest weapons come from metals mined deep in the mountains, or salvaged from places no sensible person goes. Dwarven metal, ebony, moonstone and stranger materials each have their own temper. Some need heat. Some need patience. One, if the old stories are true, needs the bones and scales of a dragon.

I have never worked dragon bone. If you bring me some, I promise to try.

#The Most Important Lesson

Keep your forge clean. Keep your tools sharp. Keep your temper cool and your fire hot, and never, ever let a customer pay you in cheese.
